_about: Raw reports behind docs/research/2026-10-02-rendering-and-import-assessment.md: four survey agents (inventory of our renderer, three.js r186, the frontier, the OBJ stress test) and a fact-check of each of the first three (status per claim with corrections and sources). Paths under /private/tmp were a session's scratch directory; the OBJ kit now lives in tools/scripts/dev/objstress and writes to build/objstress.

report.architecture:
Forward renderer, not deferred. It uses clustered (Forward+) lighting, with a G-buffer-like prepass that runs only when features need it. It sits on a very thin WebGPU layer. Code: engine/renderer/src/renderer.cpp is 13,835 lines; the whole renderer module is 17,908 lines (animation.cpp 1,462, particles.cpp 330, primitives.cpp 178, debug_draw.cpp 64). The "RHI" is engine/rhi/src/device.cpp (692 lines) plus include/pocket/rhi/device.hpp (112 lines). It only handles the device, frames, presenting and captures. renderer.cpp calls the webgpu.h C API directly (for example wgpuRenderPassEncoderDrawIndexed at renderer.cpp:12625), so there is no draw abstraction. The offscreen target is RGBA8Unorm with Depth24Plus (device.hpp:73-74). It is blitted to the surface. The HDR scene target is RGBA16Float (renderer.cpp:61). Depth is standard, not reversed: CompareFunction_Less/LessEqual only. There are 33 begin_pass/begin_compute sites and about 75 WGSL entry points embedded as raw strings. Every pass gets GPU timestamps (kTimedPasses=96, renderer.cpp:4753; rendering.md:175-185).

Frame order at HEAD a171c85a (Renderer::render_scene, renderer.cpp:11162-13410):
(0) CPU: gather lights and assign them to a 16x9x24 froxel grid. The CPU does this, max 1024 lights (renderer.cpp:30-33; rendering.md:985-999). Write one 464-byte object row per MeshRenderer submesh or sprite into a storage buffer, max 65,536 rows a frame (renderer.cpp:170-171, 11977-11979). Cull each draw on the CPU (bounding sphere vs the 6 frustum planes) and pick its LOD by screen size (renderer.cpp:12084-12118). Stable-sort by blend, cutout, skinned, material, texture and mesh (renderer.cpp:12120-12130).
(1) Sky environment compute (fill, GGX prefilter, SH9), only when the sky changes (rendering.md:336-345).
(2) Sun CSM: 4 cascades of 2048 (renderer.cpp:238, 268). Cascades are kept or amortized; about 2 of 4 are redrawn per frame (renderer.cpp:12632-12711; rendering.md:197-209). Each cascade has its own caster cull.
(3) Weather shelter map, drawn from above (renderer.cpp:12713-12766).
(4) Reflection-probe capture, at most 1 a frame: 6 views of 128 px, a panorama, prefilter and SH (renderer.cpp:12768-12971).
(5) Irradiance-volume probe captures, 2 a frame (renderer.cpp:12973-13027).
(6) Local-light shadow atlas: 4096 split into 64 faces of 512 (renderer.cpp:13029-13062).
(7) GPU particle simulation compute (renderer.cpp:13129-13156).
(8) "ids" prepass, when split: 4 MRT (R32Uint id, RG16F velocity, RGBA16F octahedral normal/roughness/metallic, RGBA8 albedo) with its own depth, then half-res AO plus contact shadows (renderer.cpp:13158-13191).
(9) Volumetric clouds at quarter resolution (renderer.cpp:13193).
(10) Scene pass. It clears its own depth and does not reuse the prepass depth (renderer.cpp:12568-12571, 13215-13235). Order inside: sky triangle, grass, opaque, cutout, skinned and user-WGSL runs; glass (copies the scene, then its own pass); sorted translucents or weighted-blended OIT; water (from copies of scene and prepass); sprites, particles, weather drops, debug lines (13237-13369).
(11) SSGI, (12) SSR, (13) TAA resolve, (14) DOF / motion blur, (15) volumetric fog at half resolution, (16) bloom (renderer.cpp:13370-13400).
(17) Final pass: exposure (auto-exposure meter compute), height fog, tonemap (none/ACES/AgX/PBR Neutral), grade and LUT, toon outlines and highlights from ids, colour-vision filter. Then user WGSL post effects. Then the spatial upscale to the window, then the UI (rendering.md:53-66, 103-127, 1068-1096).

The prepass runs when MSAA, AO, fog, SSR, SSGI, TAA, DOF, water or glass is on.

Submission: CPU-built instanced draws. Each run of equal mesh, submesh and material is one DrawIndexed with instance_index selecting the row (renderer.cpp:12583-12630; rendering.md:21-25). Indices are always Uint32 (renderer.cpp:12619, 13077, 13086). Vertices are 40 B (status.md:128). There is no DrawIndirect, multi-draw, GPU culling, Hi-Z or occlusion query, no meshlets or virtualized geometry, and no bindless (grep found none). LOD is discrete meshoptimizer simplification per draw. Terrain uses chunked LOD with skirts.

How many times geometry is drawn: a mesh is rasterized about 4 times a frame in steady state. That is the prepass, the scene pass (4x MSAA when on), and about 2 cascade redraws. Light faces, probe views (6 per capture) and the shelter map add more when they run.

features.what: Metallic-roughness PBR, lit in linear HDR
features.technique: Lambert diffuse + GGX with Schlick Fresnel and Schlick-GGX Smith k=(r+1)^2/8 (the UE4 Karis 2013 form; not height-correlated except for anisotropy). The split-sum environment term uses Karis's analytic fit (no LUT). No multi-scatter energy compensation. Diffuse sky light is SH9. Punctual lights use a windowed quadratic falloff.

features.what: Unlimited point and spot lights, 1024 nearest kept in view
features.technique: Clustered forward: 16x9x24 log-depth froxels, assigned on the CPU (sphere vs cluster AABB), max 262,144 entries
features.evidence: renderer.cpp:30-33; rendering.md:985-1031; tests/evidence/rendering/README.md (lights.png: 75 lamps + 3 spots, max 25 lights per cluster)

features.what: Cascaded shadow maps, optional PCSS and contact shadows
features.technique: 4 x 2048 cascades with log splits, texel snapping, a 10% blend band, normal offset, 3x3 PCF. PCSS: 16-tap blocker search, then 16-tap disc filter. Screen-space contact shadows: 12 steps in the AO pass. Cascades are kept across frames: redrawn only when casters, the sun or the slice change; moving casters are refreshed every 1, 2 or 4 frames by cascade.

features.what: Spot (1 face) and point (6 faces) shadows
features.technique: 4096 depth atlas of 64 x 512 faces, nearest lights first, casters culled to the light's reach, 3x3 PCF

features.what: One-bounce SSGI
features.technique: Half-res, 2 cosine rays x 12 steps marched through the prepass depth. Temporal accumulation (10% a frame) where the depth agrees. Depth-aware full-res add, albedo-modulated.

features.what: Reflection probes and irradiance volumes. Both dynamic but amortized; nothing is baked offline.
features.technique: Reflection probe: rasterized 6x128 px cube, then a 256x128 panorama with 5 GGX-prefiltered levels and SH9 diffuse, box-projected. At most 8 probes and 1 capture a frame; 3 sequential captures give 3 bounces; `realtime` probes take turns. Irradiance volume: a grid of up to 16^3 probes (1024 total, 4 volumes), each SH9 plus a 16x16 octahedral depth-moments map with a Chebyshev visibility weight (DDGI-style, but rasterized, not ray-traced). 2 probes a frame, 3 bounces.

features.what: SSR, falling back to probes, then the sky
features.technique: Mirror ray marched in screen space with 1/w depth, jittered starts and bisection. With TAA, half the steps a frame on a golden-ratio offset. Blended through the split-sum BRDF.

features.what: Half-res hemisphere SSAO
features.technique: Normal-oriented hemisphere samples from the prepass depth, 5x5 bilateral blur. Applied to ambient and environment light only.

features.what: MSAA 4x, TAA, spatial render scale
features.technique: MSAA with a separate single-sample id pass. TAA: Halton(2,3) jitter over 8 frames, per-object previous matrices give velocity, YCoCg neighbourhood clip, luma weighting, feedback 0.9; off by default. Render scale is bilinear plus a clamped 4-neighbour sharpen (spatial only), with dynamic resolution driven by GPU timestamps. No FXAA/SMAA, no temporal upscaler, no FSR/DLSS/MetalFX.

features.what: Base, metallic-roughness, normal and emissive maps; sheen, specular, anisotropy, clearcoat, transmission, IOR, volume, unlit, emissive_strength, texture_transform. Also project WGSL surface functions.
features.technique: Extensions are factors only: transmission, clearcoat, sheen, specular and anisotropy textures are not read. Sheen uses Charlie with Neubelt visibility (sun and lights only). Anisotropic GGX. Glass is screen-space refraction from a scene copy with thickness and attenuation, plus a roughness blur. No iridescence, no dispersion, no materials variants. The glTF occlusionTexture is ignored: no 'occlusion' anywhere in assets.cpp. KTX2/Basis is decoded to RGBA8, so there are no GPU-compressed formats.

features.what: Sorted alpha blending, or weighted-blended OIT
features.technique: Far-to-near sort per entity. McGuire/Bavoil WBOIT with accumulation and revealage targets, MSAA-aware

features.what: Bloom, DOF, motion blur, auto exposure, 4 tonemappers, grade, LUT, toon outlines, highlights, colour-blind filter, user WGSL post chain
features.technique: Half-res threshold with 9-tap gaussian. Thin-lens CoC with a 24-tap golden-angle gather. Velocity-based motion blur (5x5 max tile). Log-luminance meter compute. ACES fit / AgX / Khronos PBR Neutral. Machado 2009 daltonization.

features.what: Procedural, HDRI or physical atmosphere; full day-night cycle with moon and stars; aerial perspective; ray-marched volumetric clouds; rain, snow, wetness, puddles, snow cover, lightning
features.technique: Single-scattering Nishita (Rayleigh + Mie) baked into a 512x256 panorama; multiple scattering is faked by halving the view path. It is not Hillaire's LUT method. Clouds: quarter-res raymarch, 48 steps plus 5 toward the sun, a 64^3 Perlin-Worley noise volume, 3 octaves of multiple-scattering approximation, temporal reprojection. Weather: stateless vertex-shader drops, plus a shelter depth map for occlusion.

features.what: Lit height fog with light shafts from the sun and local lights
features.technique: Half-res per-pixel ray march, 16 steps with interleaved-gradient-noise offsets and temporal blend, HG phase, cascade and atlas shadow lookups, depth-aware upsample. Not froxel-based.

features.what: Lakes, rivers and an infinite ocean, shared with physics, buoyancy and swimming
features.technique: 4 Gerstner waves (no FFT) on a CPU-defined grid or camera-centred rings, plus 2 layers of procedural ripple noise for normals. Screen-space refraction and absorption, sky/probe/SSR reflections, GGX sun glint, procedural (not traced) caustics, foam from depth and crests, Snell's window underwater, splash rings and wakes as normal perturbations.

features.what: Heightfield terrain up to 1025^2 with chunked LOD; 4 splat layers with height blend; GPU grass; scattered props with sway and LOD
features.technique: Squares of 32-64 cells with error-measured LODs (under 2 px) and skirts; no geomorphing. Grass: blades generated in the vertex shader from world-locked cells (no instance buffer), thinned with distance, wind and trampling.

features.what: CPU particles (deterministic, on the sim tick) and GPU particles (compute ring of up to hundreds of thousands)
features.technique: CPU particles are instanced quads, each an object row. The GPU path simulates in compute (gravity, drag, curl turbulence, depth-buffer collision) and draws from the ring with no upload.

features.what: None
features.technique: No acceleration structures, ray queries, SDF or voxel tracing; every 'ray' is a screen-space or depth-buffer march
features.evidence: grep for ray_query/BLAS/TLAS/acceleration in engine/renderer and engine/rhi: 0 hits

features.what: None; SDR sRGB only
features.technique: 8-bit RGBA8Unorm frame, sRGB-encoded in the final pass

features.what: High-poly OBJ+MTL, STL and PLY are read natively. FBX, DAE, USD, ABC and .blend go through headless Blender to glTF. STEP, IGES and JT (industrial CAD formats) are not supported.
features.technique: Line-by-line istringstream parser with a std::map vertex dedup; Uint32 indices, so no 65k vertex limit. Missing normals are smoothed across all faces with no crease angle. One draw per (o-object, material) submesh. No automatic LOD or unit conversion on import.

performance: All numbers below are self-reported in the repo, measured on an Apple M5 MacBook (wgpu-native/Metal) via render.stats.gpu timestamps. None are on a discrete GPU or at 4K. There are no web performance numbers for 3D scenes. I did not re-run anything: the benchmark is running and the binary must not be touched.
samples/showcase at 1920x1080 (TAA, SSR, AO, volumetric fog, bloom, CSM, probe): GPU frame 5.8 ms; 3.6 ms at 0.75 render scale; 1.9 ms at 0.5 (rendering.md:123-125).

samples/hills at 1920x1080, about 1.1M triangles drawn: GPU 4.7 / 3.0 / 2.4 ms at scale 1 / 0.75 / 0.5 (rendering.md:124-125). Triangle count 1.15M after LOD, down from 1.46M (rendering.md:649-650). 971 draws frustum-culled; the cascades draw 2,242 casters instead of 4x1,341 (rendering.md:194-195).
Scene pass 1.34 ms and id pass 0.23 ms in the showcase at 1080p; hills 2.0 and 0.48 ms (rendering.md:671-673, tools/scripts/dev/gpu_probe.py).

SSR at 1080p in the showcase: about 1.0 ms with TAA step-splitting, vs 1.55 ms at 48 steps (rendering.md:718-719). SSGI at 1080p: about 1.1 ms (0.65 gather + 0.47 add) (rendering.md:752-753). Volumetric fog at 1080p: 1.9 ms at 16 steps vs 4.3 ms at 40, 'measured beside another workload' (rendering.md:962-964).
Volumetric clouds: 0.3-1.3 ms at 1280x720, 'with other GPU work running' (rendering.md:457-458).
Soft shadows (PCSS) plus contact shadows: about 0.2 ms on the showcase at 960x540 (rendering.md:526-528).
Terrain LOD, a 1025x1025 grid at 1280x720: 1.01M triangles and 2.1 ms GPU, vs 2.10M triangles and 4.9 ms as a single mesh (terrain.md:202-206).
Crowd of 256 skinned humanoids at 1280x720 with shadows: 0.92 ms CPU and 0.66 ms GPU in 41 draws (animation.md:302-306).
GPU particles, a ring of 200,000 at 1280x720: 0.74 ms CPU and 1.3 ms GPU. A CPU fountain of 20,000 took 8.7 ms CPU (particles.md:144-146).
FPS sample at 1920x1080: 4.6 ms a frame, 3.4 ms of it GPU (combat.md:79-80).
Instancing: 3,000 cubes went from 3,000 draws to 1, render cost 0.90 to 0.35 ms (status.md:21, docs/evidence/swarm.md).
Kept cascades: about 2 of 4 redrawn a frame in running samples (hills 2.0, village 2.2, farm 2.05, island 2.1) (rendering.md:206-207).

gaps.gap: No GPU-driven rendering: no indirect or multi-draw, no GPU frustum or occlusion culling (no Hi-Z, no occlusion queries), no bindless
gaps.why_it_matters: The CPU rebuilds and uploads every 464-byte object row each frame and issues one DrawIndexed per run, with a hard cap of 65,536 rows. Dense scenes (forests, cities, CAD assemblies with thousands of parts) become CPU- and draw-bound, and hidden geometry is still shaded. Unity 6 (GPU Resident Drawer plus GPU occlusion culling) and UE5 (Nanite) moved past this. So did three.js r186, which has webgpu_occlusion, webgpu_struct_drawindirect and BatchedMesh examples.
gaps.evidence: renderer.cpp:170-171, 12084-12118, 12583-12630; grep of DrawIndirect/occlusion: 0 hits. three.js r186 examples list via GitHub API (2026-10-02). Unity 6 features: https://unity.com/blog/engine-platform/unity-6-preview-release (2024).

gaps.gap: No virtualized geometry, meshlets or continuous LOD
gaps.why_it_matters: LOD is discrete meshoptimizer decimation with popping (no cross-fade or geomorph) and has to be opted into per entity. High-poly imports draw at full density until someone sets MeshRenderer.lods. This is the single biggest gap to UE5 Nanite, which since 5.7 also covers foliage.

gaps.gap: Redundant rasterization: the prepass depth is not reused by the scene pass
gaps.why_it_matters: The ids prepass writes its own Depth32F, then the scene pass clears a separate depth and re-rasterizes everything with LESS. Overdraw in the lit pass is not removed by a depth-equal pass. Apple's tile-based hidden-surface removal hides some of this; discrete desktop GPUs and the web will pay for it.

gaps.gap: No ray tracing and no world-space dynamic GI at scale
gaps.why_it_matters: GI is one-bounce SSGI (it misses off-screen and occluded light) plus rasterized probes amortized at 1-2 captures a frame, capped at 8 reflection probes and 1024 grid probes. That is nowhere near Lumen (software or hardware RT GI and reflections) or HDRP's RTGI, RT reflections, or APV with sky occlusion and scenario blending. Local light shadows are also missing from probe captures.

gaps.gap: No temporal upscaler; TAA is off by default; no specular anti-aliasing
gaps.why_it_matters: Render scale is bilinear plus sharpen only, versus UE TSR, Unity STP, and three.js r186's own TAAUNode and FSR1Node. The island sample ships MSAA without TAA, hills ships no AA at all, and no Toksvig/Kaplanyan-style roughness filtering exists. The result is visible specular shimmer and black dashes on the ocean (island.png, ocean.png).
gaps.evidence: renderer.cpp:500-513; rendering.md:917-919; samples/island/project.toml [render]; grep toksvig/kaplanyan/fwidth-roughness: 0 hits; three.js examples/jsm/tsl/display/TAAUNode.js@r186

gaps.gap: Material coverage below three.js and glTF PBR Next
gaps.why_it_matters: Transmission, clearcoat, sheen, specular and anisotropy textures are ignored (factors only). No iridescence, dispersion or materials variants. The glTF occlusionTexture (baked AO) is ignored. Sheen is not lit by the sky, and there is no multi-scatter compensation. There is no SSS, hair or eye shading and no layered material (UE Substrate became production-ready in 5.7). three.js MeshPhysicalMaterial has all of these plus maps for each.
gaps.evidence: assets.md:382-387; rendering.md:578-581, 1102-1103; grep 'occlusion' in engine/assets/src/assets.cpp: 0 hits; https://threejs.org/docs/pages/MeshPhysicalMaterial.html (fetched 2026-10-02)

gaps.gap: No GPU texture compression and no streaming
gaps.why_it_matters: KTX2/Basis is transcoded to RGBA8 on load, and terrain layers are resampled to 512. VRAM and bandwidth grow linearly with content, and there is no virtual texturing or texture streaming for large worlds.

gaps.gap: Shadows are fixed-resolution; no area lights
gaps.why_it_matters: 4x2048 cascades and 512 px local faces (64 max), compared with UE Virtual Shadow Maps and MegaLights (stochastic many-light shadows, beta in 5.7). There are no rect or area lights (no LTC). Glass casts a whole shadow.

gaps.gap: Atmosphere and water are simplified models
gaps.why_it_matters: The atmosphere is single-scattering Nishita baked into a panorama, not a Hillaire-style multi-scattering LUT with froxel aerial perspective. Environment reflections do not show volumetric clouds. Water is 4 Gerstner waves plus noise (no FFT spectrum), with procedural caustics and only rectangle or ribbon shapes. UE and HDRP ship FFT water and LUT atmospheres.
The 8-bit sRGB swapchain wastes the HDR pipeline on HDR-capable Mac and phone displays.
A 1025^2 grid at most, no streaming, no LOD blending, 4 layers, no per-layer normal or roughness maps. Large open worlds need multiple hand-placed terrains.

gaps.gap: Industrial high-poly OBJ path is functional but unoptimized (partly unverified)
gaps.why_it_matters: Import works with Uint32 indices. However, the parser tokenizes every line through istringstream into std::vector<std::string> and dedups vertices with std::map, which will likely be slow on multi-million-triangle OBJs; this is not benchmarked, so it is unverified. Missing normals are smoothed with no crease angle, which rounds off CAD hard edges. STEP, IGES and JT are not supported. Every (object, material) group becomes its own draw and object row, which interacts badly with the 65,536-row cap. There is no automatic LOD, meshlets or unit (mm) handling.

Every number comes from one Apple M5 under wgpu-native/Metal, at 720p or 1080p, sometimes 'beside another workload'. There are no discrete-GPU, 4K, browser-WebGPU or side-by-side engine comparisons, so the 'how fast compared to X' claims cannot be made yet.

report.honest_quality_verdict:
I viewed 14 evidence PNGs: showcase, pbr, materials, island (plus a 2x crop), ocean, clouds, glass, irradiance, ssr, probes, grass, atmosphere, village-day (plus a crop of the dusk panel) and fps.

**Feature list.** It is a broad, coherent forward+ list, roughly where AAA forward renderers were around 2016-2019: clustered lights, CSM with PCSS, SSAO, SSR, TAA, probe GI, volumetric fog. On top of that it has ray-marched clouds, DDGI-style probe visibility, and an integrated sky, weather, water and terrain stack. Lighting is physically consistent: HDR with AgX, and sky light that agrees with the sun across a full day.

**Where the images are good.**
- The volumetric clouds are the strongest element. The fair-weather and rain decks in clouds.png and ocean.png are respectable even at a casual glance next to Unity HDRP.
- grass.png and the noon panel of clouds.png read as a pleasant stylized indie scene.
- glass.png shows correct inverted refraction through the thick ball and a nice clear-coat highlight.

**Where they are weak.** Mostly this is content: primitive boxes, lollipop trees, low-poly props, and procedural or checker textures instead of authored PBR texture sets. But several artifacts are technical:
- Ocean (island.png, ocean.png): severe specular aliasing. There are black horizontal dashes and pixel noise toward the horizon, and the near water looks like a noisy normal map rather than a sea surface. There is no specular AA, and the island sample runs without TAA.
- probes.png: reflections are blocky and low-res (128 px faces), with a smeared, misregistered box-projected crate reflection and a noisy ceiling blob.
- ssr.png: the orb's reflection is blurry and dim, and the procedural sky shows a flat grey "ground" band with a hard edge at the horizon (also in materials.png).
- village-day.png: the dusk frames have large hard-edged dark wedges and grain on the grass (cause not verified), plus a dark band at the world's edge.
- showcase.png: fog washes the whole frame to near-monochrome beige over untextured geometry. The light shafts on the floor are nice, but the frame does not sell the feature list.
- irradiance.png: the colour bleed is correct but faint, and the room looks flat.
- pbr.png and materials.png look like test scenes, not showcases.

**Against UE5 (5.7: Lumen, Nanite, VSM, TSR, Substrate, MegaLights).** Not in the same class. It is a generation or more behind in GI quality, geometric density, shadow resolution and upscaling, and the images read like a UE4-era or Unity built-in-pipeline stylized demo, not a modern photoreal frame.

**Against three.js r186 (2026-09-24).** On paper the technique lists are now close: three.js ships SSGI, SSR, GTAO, TRAA, TAAU, FSR1, clustered lights, probe grids, CSM and OIT as TSL add-ons. three.js is ahead on material extensions (iridescence, dispersion, all the maps, AO maps), compressed textures, temporal upscaling and GPU-driven primitives. aipocket is ahead on integration: everything is a component field, it is deterministic and inspectable by an agent, and it has built-in atmosphere, day-night, weather, ocean, terrain and grass systems coupled to physics, which three.js leaves to the user.

**Overall judgement (mine, not measured).** The best artist-made three.js showcase sites look better than these evidence images. That gap comes mostly from authored assets, baked lighting and AA or specular filtering, not from missing passes.

**Highest-leverage fixes for visible quality:**
1. TAA on by default plus specular AA for water and normal maps.
2. A temporal upscaler.
3. Higher-resolution or SSR-blended probes.
4. A real asset and texture pass on the showcase scenes.
5. GPU-driven culling and indirect draws before attempting high-poly CAD scenes.

The lit shader walks the whole list per pixel instead of clustering it, which is a cost the report also misses.

Also missing: 2D lights with occluder-map shadows for orthographic games (renderer.cpp:1404-1407 shadow_2d, 1595, 4527 gather_occluders), and render-to-texture / secondary views such as split screen, minimaps and in-world screens, where TAA and the fog history are switched off (renderer.cpp:11163-11195, 11031 view_texture).

Culling details that matter for the user's CAD question: all submeshes of an entity share one Bounds sphere; skinned and unbounded draws are never frustum-culled (renderer.cpp:11735-11736, 11876-11879); and the 65,536-row cap counts off-screen draws too, then silently drops the rest (11750, 11790, 12066).

TAA motion vectors ignore skinning: a skinned mesh's joints are followed only as far as its entity moves (rendering.md:916-917). Animated characters will ghost or smear under TAA, which matters for the report's recommendation to turn TAA on by default.

Probe and volume selection: the lit pass takes the first probe by entity id whose box holds the point, with no blending between overlapping probes, only a half-unit fade (rendering.md:780-783); irradiance volumes likewise take 'the first by id where boxes overlap' (engine/world/meta/components.toml:149).

Depth precision: the frame depth is non-reversed Depth24Plus, the island camera has far=1500 (samples/island/scene.json) with a default near of 0.1 (components.toml:83), and the ocean's horizon ring is drawn just inside the far plane (water.md:105-107). This is a plausible contributor to far-water and horizon artifacts that the report never considers.

three.js r186 also ships world-space voxel GI (examples/jsm/lighting/vxgi/VXGINode.js, webgpu_vxgi.html, webgpu_vxgi_sponza.html), RectAreaLight (webgpu_lights_rectarealight.html), SMAA and FXAA nodes, and Gaussian-splat loaders (SPZ, KSPLAT, GaussianSplatPLYLoader). The 'technique lists are now close' comparison therefore understates three.js on GI and area lights, which are exactly aipocket's gaps.

For the industrial-import question: three.js r186 has 3DMLoader (Rhino), 3MFLoader, AMFLoader, VRMLLoader and VTKLoader, but no STEP or IGES either. A STEP path in either engine needs OpenCascade or occt-import-js, or an offline conversion (unverified beyond the loader list at tag r186).

Import pipeline gaps for high-poly OBJ: no vertex-cache, overdraw or fetch optimization (the only meshoptimizer calls are simplifyWithAttributes and decode*); `s` smoothing groups are ignored; after the first `o`, `g` groups do not create nodes (import.cpp:173-174); n-gons are fanned, so concave faces triangulate wrongly (import.cpp:183); and OBJ is re-parsed on every load with no cache (assets.cpp:2107-2112).

Unverified platform context: core browser WebGPU has DrawIndexedIndirect and compute but, as far as I know, no bindless or multi-draw-indirect, so GPU-driven rendering on the web build would need one indirect draw per batch. The report recommends GPU-driven culling without noting this constraint.
Translucent meshes in front of water are hidden by the water surface (water.md:251-252). This is a visible correctness gap not listed among the renderer gaps.

capabilities.what: There are two renderers. `import 'three'` still resolves to build/three.module.js with WebGLRenderer. WebGPURenderer needs the separate entry point `three/webgpu`, and TSL comes from `three/tsl` (package.json exports at r186). WebGPURenderer runs a WebGPU backend and falls back to a WebGL 2 backend automatically; `forceWebGL` forces the fallback. The official manual still says: "The renderer itself is still in an experimental state although its maturity level has been greatly improved in the last years." It also says that, depending on the scene, you may hit missing features or get better performance with WebGLRenderer. WebGLRenderer is "still maintained" but there are "no plans to add larger new features" to it. So WebGPURenderer is not the default and is not officially declared production-ready. Third-party blogs disagree: utsubo.com (2026) calls it "recommended since r171 (September 2025)" and production-ready. That is wrong on the facts, because the GitHub API dates r171 to 2024-11-29 (it introduced the three/webgpu code split). Treat those blogs as unreliable.

TSL (Three Shading Language) is a JavaScript node DSL that compiles to WGSL (WebGPU backend) or GLSL (WebGL2 fallback). It has node versions of every material: MeshStandard/Physical/Lambert/Phong/Toon/Matcap/Basic NodeMaterial, plus MeshSSSNodeMaterial, VolumeNodeMaterial, ShadowNodeMaterial, Line2NodeMaterial and Points/Sprite. ShaderMaterial, RawShaderMaterial and onBeforeCompile are not supported under WebGPURenderer, so custom materials have to be ported to TSL. r186 added TSL GPU unit tests, a 'Tour of TSL' doc, atomic workgroup arrays, subgroup fixes, and an Inspector addon with a TSL graph editor and timeline. Earlier releases also ship a GLSL-to-TSL transpiler addon.
capabilities.source: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/tree/r186/src/materials/nodes ; manual webgpurenderer.html (Migration section); https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/releases/tag/r186 (Nodes / Inspector / Transpiler sections)

capabilities.what: MeshStandardMaterial uses metal/rough GGX. MeshPhysicalMaterial adds clearcoat (with roughness and normal maps), sheen (color and roughness), transmission with thickness/attenuationColor/attenuationDistance (volume), iridescence (IOR and thickness range), anisotropy (with rotation and map), dispersion, specularIntensity/specularColor, ior, and retroreflectivity (new in r186, PR #33949, with environment-lighting support). r186 also fixed multiscatter energy compensation, iridescence IBL multiscatter, and diffuse/sheen energy conservation. Transmission is screen-space, not ray-traced: WebGLRenderer renders opaque objects into a mip-mapped transmission render target and samples it (renderTransmissionPass, WebGLRenderer.js L2002-2017). Tone mappers: Linear, Reinhard, Cineon, ACESFilmic, AgX, Neutral and Custom. The renderer default is NoToneMapping.

Shadow map types (constants.js r186 L57-84): BasicShadowMap, PCFShadowMap, PCFSoftShadowMap (deprecated in r186: use PCFShadowMap, which uses textureGatherCompare on WebGPU since r185) and VSMShadowMap. Directional, spot and point lights cast shadows, and WebGPU has shadow-map arrays. Cascaded shadows are not part of core DirectionalLight. They come from addons: (1) CSM for WebGLRenderer; (2) CSMShadowNode for WebGPURenderer, with 3 cascades by default and practical/uniform/logarithmic/custom splits; (3) the new SunLight addon (r186), which has built-in CSM fixed at 2 cascades ('Reduce cascade count to 2'), 1024² per cascade, and cascade fade blending. SunLight works on WebGL, and on WebGPU it must be registered with renderer.library.addLight. Other addons: TileShadowNode (tiled shadow maps, no VSM) and SSSNode (screen-space contact shadows). PCSS exists only as an example (webgl_shadowmap_pcss), and ProgressiveLightMap is an addon.
capabilities.built_in_or_addon: core (basic/PCF/VSM); addons (CSM, SunLight, tiled, PCSS example)

capabilities.what: There are two separate stacks. WebGLRenderer uses EffectComposer and passes in examples/jsm/postprocessing: UnrealBloomPass, SSAOPass, SAOPass, GTAOPass, SSRPass, BokehPass, TAARenderPass, SMAAPass, FXAAPass, OutlinePass, LUTPass and others. WebGPURenderer uses RenderPipeline (renamed from PostProcessing in r183), which has built-in MRT and automatic pass merging. Its effects are TSL nodes in examples/jsm/tsl/display: GTAONode, SSAONode (new in r186), SSGINode (added 2025-09-08, based on SSRT3/SSILVB), SSRNode (single-ray mode or stochastic GGX mode with an SSR denoiser), TRAANode, TAAUNode (r184 temporal upsampling), FSR1Node, SMAA, FXAA, SSAA, BloomNode (selective bloom via an emissive MRT), DepthOfFieldNode (bokeh), MotionBlur (from a velocity MRT), GodraysNode, LensflareNode, OITPassNode (weighted-blended OIT, r186), Lut3D, Outline, Denoise and RecurrentDenoise, SSSNode, plus a set of blurs. EffectComposer does not work with WebGPURenderer. The manual says SSGI, SSS and the better DoF exist only for WebGPURenderer. All of these are addons, not core.

Core rendering is forward. ClusteredLighting (Forward+ clustered shading, added to the WebGPURenderer addons 2026-04-22 in r185) is an opt-in replacement via renderer.lighting. DynamicLighting is an addon that batches analytic lights into uniform arrays so light-count changes don't trigger recompiles. Core lights: Ambient, Hemisphere, Directional, Point, Spot, RectArea (LTC), LightProbe. WebGPU-only core lights: IESSpotLight and ProjectorLight. Deferred shading appears only as an example ('Simple deferred rendering using custom pipeline', webgpu_deferred, r186), not as a renderer mode. Volumetric lighting uses VolumeNodeMaterial (webgpu_volume_lighting*), and height fog and custom fog are available as TSL examples.
capabilities.built_in_or_addon: core forward; clustered/dynamic lighting are addons; deferred is example-only

capabilities.what: Core has no real-time GI. Core does provide image-based lighting through PMREM (r186 replaced the separable blur with a spiral blur), single LightProbe spherical harmonics, and material lightMap/aoMap for externally baked lightmaps. Addons add: (1) LightProbeGrid (2026-04-16, r184), position-dependent diffuse GI from a baked SH irradiance volume, with incremental baking in r186 and separate WebGL and WebGPU versions; (2) VXGINode (2026-08-31, r186), voxel cone tracing for diffuse GI and AO. VXGINode's header says it is only for WebGPURenderer with a WebGPU backend, that objects should stay static because re-voxelization is too expensive per frame, that only direct lights are injected, and that resolution should not exceed 256; (3) SSGINode (screen-space); (4) ProgressiveLightMap/ProgressiveLightMapGPU, which accumulates lightmaps in the browser. Specular GI is limited to SSR plus IBL, and there is no hardware ray tracing.
capabilities.built_in_or_addon: addon (core only has IBL, a single SH probe, and baked lightmaps)

capabilities.what: Sky (WebGL) and SkyMesh (WebGPU) implement the Preetham analytic daylight model. A procedural cloud layer was added in r183 and made 'more realistic' in r186. It is a 2D fbm layer projected from direction.xz/direction.y (SkyMesh.js ~L330-376), not volumetric. Volumetric clouds exist only as raymarched 3D-texture examples (webgl/webgpu_volume_cloud). The 3D-tiles example gets physical atmosphere and volumetric clouds from third-party packages (@takram/three-atmosphere 0.19.1 with Bruneton precomputation, and @takram/three-clouds 0.7.6), not from three.js. Water options: Water/WaterMesh (flat planar-reflection water with normal maps), Water2/Water2Mesh (flow-map water), webgpu_compute_water (compute heightfield), and webgpu_ocean (WaterMesh + SkyMesh). I found no FFT/spectral ocean addon in the r186 file list (unverified beyond the listing).
capabilities.built_in_or_addon: addon / examples; physical atmosphere and volumetric clouds are third-party

capabilities.what: Core InstancedMesh, and core BatchedMesh (multi-draw: many geometries and instances under one material, with per-instance frustum culling and sorting; r186 added batchIndirectIndex in TSL). Core LOD is basic discrete distance switching with manually supplied levels. The library has no automatic LOD generation. SimplifyModifier is a CPU addon, and the progressive-LOD example uses the external @needle-tools/gltf-progressive. webgpu_compute_rasterizer (renamed from 'nanite-style' in r185) demonstrates meshlet visibility buffers with software rasterization of small triangles, but it is an example, not an engine feature. WebGPURenderer supports occlusion queries (r186 fixes #33959 and #33972), and culling is per-object on the CPU.

WebGPURenderer runs TSL compute (Fn().compute(), renderer.compute, plus compileComputeAsync in r186) with storage buffers and textures, atomics, subgroups and workgroup arrays. The GPGPU addons include BitonicSort and CountingSort, and r186 ships about 18 webgpu_compute_* examples (particles, cloth, water, sorting, rasterizer). On the WebGL2 fallback, compute is emulated with transform feedback. WebGLBackend.compute (L918-982) warns that the count must be a single number and that indirect counts are not supported.
capabilities.source: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/r186/src/renderers/webgl-fallback/WebGLBackend.js#L918 ; examples/files.json at r186; r186 release notes (#32551)

capabilities.what: Core has neither. three-gpu-pathtracer (gkjohnson, MIT, separate project) released v0.0.25 on 2026-09-28. That release added WebGPUPathTracer ('three-gpu-pathtracer/webgpu', WebGPU compute), deprecated WebGLPathTracer, and requires three r185 or later. v0.0.26 followed on 2026-09-29. According to its README it needs WebGPU, supports only Standard/Physical materials, and uses MIS for lights. It is built on three-mesh-bvh (v0.9.15, 2026-09-09). Path tracing is progressive offline-quality rendering, not real-time game RT. The three.js editor has a path-trace viewport mode that uses WebGLPathTracer (editor/js/Viewport.Pathtracer.js at r186).

GLTFLoader supports KHR_draco_mesh_compression (DRACOLoader, WASM in workers), EXT_meshopt_compression and KHR_meshopt_compression (r183), KHR_texture_basisu (KTX2Loader with a Basis transcoder in workers), KHR_mesh_quantization, EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing, KHR_materials_* (clearcoat, dispersion, ior, sheen, specular, transmission, iridescence, anisotropy, unlit, volume, emissive_strength), EXT_materials_bump, EXT_texture_webp and EXT_texture_avif (GLTFLoader.js L629-652). Other loaders: OBJLoader with MTLLoader; FBXLoader (r186: multiple clips per timeline); USDLoader (USD/USDA/USDC/USDZ, with USDZLoader deprecated since r179); Rhino3dmLoader (rhino3dm.js 8.32.1 WASM in workers, where Brep faces use face.getMesh(MeshType.Any), the render meshes cached in the file, L1616-1644); 3MF, AMF, Collada, STL, PLY, VTK, PCD, XYZ, LDraw, VRML, 3DS, VOX, MaterialX; Gaussian splats (GaussianSplatPLYLoader, SPZ v4, KSPLAT, SPLAT and a glTF extension, all new in r186). IFC is shown through an example that calls web-ifc directly. three.js has no STEP/IGES/JT loader. occt-import-js (kovacsv, LGPL-2.1, Emscripten build of OpenCascade, last release v0.0.23 on 2024-12-03) turns STEP/IGES/BREP into triangulated JSON 'compatible with three.js' and powers Online 3D Viewer (MIT, last pushed 2026-06-24). Massive or streamed meshes rely on the external 3d-tiles-renderer.

OBJLoader at r186: (1) It loads the whole file as one JS string through FileLoader (L491), then parses it synchronously on the calling thread with text.split('\n') (L555). There is no worker or streaming path. (2) It pushes values into plain JS number arrays and only at the end copies them into Float32BufferAttribute (L789). (3) It emits non-indexed geometry: addVertex copies all three positions of every triangle (L235-241), so vertex count is 3 × triangle count. (4) When the file has no `vn` it generates flat per-face normals (addFaceNormal L274-293, called at L361), so smooth shading needs BufferGeometryUtils.mergeVertices plus computeVertexNormals afterwards. (5) It fan-triangulates n-gons from the first vertex (L638-653). My inference: that is wrong for concave polygons. V8 caps strings at 2^29−24 characters, so by inference (not tested) Chromium cannot hold an ASCII OBJ larger than about 512 MB as one string. Maintainer Mugen87 on the forum (2019-04): OBJLoader is not optimized for these file sizes, and binary glTF plus Draco is faster and more memory-friendly. The manual recommends glTF and lists OBJ2GLTF. The practical three.js route for CAD high-poly meshes is an offline conversion to glTF (obj2gltf or gltf-transform with weld, simplify and meshopt/Draco) and then GLTFLoader.

The README describes three.js as an "easy-to-use, lightweight, cross-browser, general-purpose 3D library". Core includes the scene graph, cameras, the animation system (AnimationMixer, skinning, morphs), WebAudio wrappers (Audio, PositionalAudio), raycasting and WebXR (WebXR on WebGPU arrived in r185). Core has no physics engine. The physics addons are thin wrappers around Ammo.js, Jolt and Rapier (manual 'Physics' page). Core also has no ECS or game framework, no navmesh, no terrain system (terrain exists only in examples), no asset pipeline or build/cook step, and no prefab system. The editor (threejs.org/editor) is a basic web scene editor. It can import about 25 formats (editor/js/Loader.js at r186), attach scripts, switch between WebGL and WebGPU renderers, and run a path-trace viewport.

notable_limits: WebGPURenderer is still officially 'experimental' (manual, last changed 2026-07-12). The default `three` import is still WebGLRenderer. Blog claims that it is 'production-ready since r171 (September 2025)' contradict the GitHub API, which dates r171 to 2024-11-29.

Almost every advanced feature is an addon or example, not core: CSM, SunLight, SSAO/GTAO, SSR, SSGI, VXGI, TRAA/TAAU, bloom, DoF, motion blur, OIT, clustered lighting, Sky, Water, LightProbeGrid. Quality varies, and the API changes every release (see the Migration Guide).

The new features are concentrated in the WebGPU/TSL path. WebGLRenderer gets 'no larger new features'. VXGINode requires the WebGPU backend specifically, and ShaderMaterial, onBeforeCompile and EffectComposer don't work under WebGPURenderer.

No real-time dynamic GI that is both robust and off-screen-aware. SSGI is screen-space, VXGI assumes static geometry and is diffuse-only, and LightProbeGrid and lightmaps are baked. There is no hardware ray tracing (WebGPU has no RT API), and path tracing is external and progressive.
Cascaded shadows come only from addons, and the SunLight addon is fixed at 2 cascades. PCSS exists only as an example.
No virtualized geometry, no automatic LOD generation and no GPU-driven culling in core. LOD is manual discrete switching. The meshlet/software-raster compute demo is an example only.
On the WebGL2 fallback, compute is emulated through transform feedback, with no indirect dispatch and a single-number count.

OBJLoader is unsuited to industrial high-poly meshes: it is synchronous on the calling thread, string-based, produces non-indexed output (3× vertices), falls back to flat normals when `vn` is missing, and fan-triangulates n-gons. Under the V8 string cap (2^29−24 chars), ASCII files above about 512 MB can't be loaded as one string (inferred, not tested). The recommended path is offline conversion to glTF with Draco or meshopt.

three.js has no STEP/IGES/JT/Parasolid import. The external occt-import-js is LGPL-2.1 and has had no release since 2024-12-03. Rhino3dmLoader meshes Breps from the render meshes cached in the .3dm file. Inference, unverified at runtime: files saved without render meshes give empty Breps.
It is a rendering library, not an engine: no built-in physics (only wrappers for Ammo, Jolt and Rapier), no ECS, navmesh, asset cooking or prefabs, and a basic editor.

Not verified by running anything: none of the examples were run and no performance was measured. Feature descriptions come from r186 source headers, release notes and the manual. A WebFetch summary of r185 claimed a '3.0x TSL compilation speed increase'; that wording is absent from the raw notes and was discarded.
report.summary:
The latest three.js release is r186. It first shipped as npm three@0.186.0 on 2026-09-08, then was re-tagged as "r186 (bis)" and published as the GitHub release and npm 0.186.1 on 2026-09-24. The dev branch is now 187dev.

**Renderer status:** three.js has two renderers. WebGLRenderer is still the default import and is in maintenance mode. WebGPURenderer (`three/webgpu`) falls back to WebGL2 automatically and uses TSL node materials, which compile to WGSL or GLSL. The official manual (last changed July 2026) still calls WebGPURenderer "experimental", so it is neither the default nor officially production-ready. Nearly all new rendering work lands on the WebGPU/TSL side.

**Built in vs addon:** Core has a full glTF-grade PBR model in MeshPhysicalMaterial: clearcoat, sheen, transmission and volume, iridescence, anisotropy, dispersion, specular, and retroreflectivity (new in r186). It also has basic, PCF and VSM shadow maps, InstancedMesh, BatchedMesh, discrete LOD, PMREM image-based lighting, and LightProbe and lightMap support. Everything beyond that is an addon or example rather than core, including:
- **Cascaded shadows:** the CSM addon, CSMShadowNode, and the new SunLight with 2 cascades.
- **Post-processing:** a node-based RenderPipeline (renamed from PostProcessing in r183) with GTAO, SSAO, SSR (including a stochastic mode with a denoiser), SSGI, TRAA, TAAU, FSR1, bloom, DoF, motion blur, godrays and weighted-blended OIT. WebGLRenderer keeps the older EffectComposer.
- **Lighting:** Forward+ ClusteredLighting.
- **GI:** LightProbeGrid (baked SH irradiance volume) and VXGINode (voxel cone tracing; WebGPU only, static geometry, diffuse only).
- **Sky and water:** a Preetham sky with a 2D cloud layer, and planar or flow-map water. Physical atmosphere and volumetric clouds come from the third-party @takram packages.

Compute is first-class on WebGPU and emulated through transform feedback on WebGL2. Path tracing lives in the separate three-gpu-pathtracer project, which got a WebGPU path tracer in v0.0.25 (2026-09-28).

**Loaders:** GLTFLoader supports Draco, meshopt (EXT and KHR) and KTX2. There are also FBX, USD/USDZ, 3DM (Rhino via rhino3dm WASM), 3MF, STL, PLY, Gaussian splats and more. There is no STEP or IGES loader; occt-import-js (LGPL, last release Dec 2024) fills that gap externally.

**High-poly OBJ:** OBJLoader handles it poorly. It parses the whole file as one string on the calling thread, outputs non-indexed geometry with 3 vertices per triangle, uses flat normals when `vn` is missing, and fan-triangulates n-gons. The maintainer recommends converting to binary glTF with Draco or meshopt instead.

**Scope:** three.js describes itself as a general-purpose 3D library, not an engine. Physics exists only as wrappers around Ammo, Jolt and Rapier, and there is no ECS, asset pipeline or prefab system. The editor is a basic web scene editor that imports about 25 formats, switches between the two renderers and has a path-trace viewport.

The 's' smoothing groups only toggle material flat shading; normals stay per-face, so the result still looks faceted. 'usemap' is unsupported.

Peak-memory reasoning for large OBJs: the whole-file string, the JS number arrays (with 3x vertex duplication from non-indexed output) and the final Float32Arrays all coexist. This inference (not tested) suggests memory is a tighter limit than the 512 MB string cap.

No performance numbers at all: no frame times, draw-call limits or triangle-throughput figures for WebGPURenderer versus WebGLRenderer. That leaves nothing quantitative to compare with aipocket's renderer.

WebGPU reach gaps for the web target: per the gpuweb wiki, edited 2026-10-02, Firefox has not shipped WebGPU on Linux or Android, and Safari 26 on macOS has it on by default only on macOS 26 Tahoe. On those browsers, WebGPURenderer runs on its WebGL2 fallback, where VXGI and indirect compute are unavailable.

5.6: hardware ray tracing (HWRT) work aimed at 60 Hz. 5.7: Epic is consolidating on HWRT and has deprecated the software-ray-tracing detail traces. 5.8 adds Lumen Lite. The release notes describe it as 'a new medium-quality setting for Global Illumination using Irradiance Fields with Probe Occlusion supported by Lumen'. It is about 2x faster than Lumen High (which targets 60fps on PS5) and is the default on handhelds. That is a DDGI-class probe method, the same family as aipocket's IrradianceVolume. Secondary sources call Lumen Lite Beta; the primary page only says 'new'.

capabilities.what: Stochastic direct lighting that importance-samples lights. It traces a fixed number of rays per pixel: a short screen-space ray first, then hardware or software ray tracing, then a denoiser. Status: Beta in 5.6 and 5.7 (5.7 added directional, Niagara and translucency lights), Production Ready in 5.8 ('Megalights is now entering Production Ready status'). It targets current-gen consoles and RT-capable PCs; mobile, Switch and last-gen are not supported. Epic recommends hardware RT.

5.7 added Nanite Foliage, Nanite Voxels and Nanite Assemblies: dense foliage built from branch building blocks, voxelized at distance, with no hand-made LODs. Foliage wind moved from world-position offset to skinned Nanite through a Dynamic Wind plugin. Nanite Foliage is Experimental in 5.7, and secondary sources say it is still Experimental in 5.8. In 5.8, tessellation in Virtual Shadow Maps (VSM) can be toggled by CVar and handhelds get faster raster and culling. The official status of Nanite tessellation/displacement is unverified; forum threads report 5.8 regressions.

5.7 turns on receiver masks for directional lights by default (a large win with dynamic geometry for about 10 MB). 5.8 adds invalidation throttling, temporal reprojection and an experimental 'Prefiltered Distant' mode for far casters.

capabilities.area: UE Substrate, TSR, path tracer, heterogeneous volumes, water and sky
capabilities.what: Substrate became fully production-ready in 5.7, and 5.8 can import X-Rite AxF measured materials into it. Temporal Super Resolution (TSR): 5.8 adds thin-geometry optimizations and fixes for camera cuts. The path tracer stays the offline-quality reference; the 5.8 notes point artists to it for filmic depth of field. Heterogeneous Volumes (OpenVDB sparse volume textures and Niagara Fluids, real-time and in the path tracer) is still Experimental in the 5.8 docs. The 5.8 notes mention neither Water nor Sky Atmosphere, so I found nothing new there (unverified).

Adaptive Probe Volumes (APV) place probes automatically, light per pixel, stream, and support lighting scenarios such as time of day. The GPU Resident Drawer uses BatchRendererGroup to do GPU instancing; it needs compute shaders and the Forward+ or Deferred+ path. Spatial-Temporal Post-Processing (STP) is a temporal upscaler that needs Shader Model 5.0 and does not run on GLES. All three arrived in Unity 6.0 and are documented under 6.6.

6.3 LTS (Dec 2025): a unified render graph and hybrid 2D/3D. 6.5 (2026-06-15): the Built-in pipeline (BIRP) is deprecated, HDRP moves to maintenance mode, and URP gets on-tile HDR on Metal and Vulkan. 6.6 (2026-09-01): WebGPU is production-ready for web builds (compute, GPU skinning, indirect draws, VFX Graph), DXC with Shader Model 6 on DX12, and a compute light baker on a unified ray-tracing API. Roadmap: 6.7 LTS brings URP 'Surface Cache GI', SSR, GTAO and unified DLSS4/FSR/PSSR upscalers; Unity 7 beta Dec 2026, release Q1 2027.

capabilities.what: Cooperative vectors arrived in DirectX Shader Model 6.9 (Agility SDK 1.619) for neural texture compression (NTC) and neural radiance caching (NRC). At GDC 2026 Microsoft announced DXR 2.0, due with SM 6.10: clustered geometry, partitioned TLAS and indirect acceleration-structure ops; it has not shipped. NVIDIA showed NTC cutting a demo's VRAM from 6.5 GB to 970 MB; NTC 0.10 beta is in RTX Kit 2026.3 (secondary sources). I found no shipped game using NTC or neural shaders. Metal 4 at WWDC26 (session 359) covers a MetalFX denoiser/upscaler, an ML command encoder and TensorOps networks inside shaders, on M5 and A19 Pro, whose GPU cores each carry a neural accelerator.

Cluster acceleration structures (CLAS) and partitioned TLAS, exposed through VK_NV_cluster_acceleration_structure and VK_NV_partitioned_acceleration_structure. Alan Wake 2 was the first game to ship it (2025-01-30). GDC 2026 showed Mega Geometry foliage, including a Witcher 4 forest (secondary source).

The exact ratification date is unverified; the README was last touched 2026-09-03. three.js r186 (2026-09-24) merged a native WebGPU/TSL splat renderer: a compute counting sort, SH0 colour only, no LOD. capabilities.what: Bevy Solari (0.17, 2025-09-30) does real-time ReSTIR DI/GI plus a world-space irradiance cache, all through inline ray queries (wgpu had no RT pipelines then), with DLSS-RR as the denoiser. On an RTX 3080 at 1600x900 upscaled to 3200x1800 it ran 8.2-14.6 ms. The author's post says it 'currently requires an NVIDIA GPU'; Metal support is unverified. Bevy 0.19 (2026-06-19) added contact shadows, GPU light clustering, Linearly Transformed Cosines (LTC) area lights, physically based SSR and parallax-corrected cubemaps. Bevy's virtual geometry (meshlets) has had BVH culling since 0.17.

Forward renderer on WebGPU. Clustered point and spot lights with a shadow atlas (rendering.md:985-1032). Four 2048 sun cascades, kept between frames (rendering.md:26-36, 197-206). Percentage-closer soft shadows (PCSS) and contact shadows (494-529). SSR (701-728). SSGI with one screen-space bounce, about 1.1 ms (729-760). Reflection probes (761-801). DDGI-style irradiance volumes captured by raster at 2 probes a frame; they settle after 3 passes and stay static until refreshed, with at most 1024 probes and 4 volumes (802-854). TAA with no upscaling (901-926); render scale is a bilinear-plus-sharpen stretch (103-128). meshoptimizer LODs (634-654). Atmosphere, day cycle, weather and clouds (252-464). Volumetric light, depth of field, motion blur, AgX, bloom. Not yet: HDR display output and others (1098-1105). The showcase runs 5.8 ms at 1080p on the M5, 1.9 ms at half scale (rendering.md:120-122). No energy-compensation, specular-occlusion or GTAO term shows up by name in engine/renderer/src/renderer.cpp (name grep only).

report.summary:
Where the frontier is on 2026-10-02:
- **UE 5.8** (2026-06-17), the last UE5 release:
  - Lumen leans on hardware ray tracing. 5.7 deprecated the software detail traces.
  - New Lumen Lite: probe GI ('Irradiance Fields with Probe Occlusion'), about 2x cheaper than Lumen High.
  - MegaLights (stochastic, ray-traced direct lighting) is production-ready.
  - Nanite Foliage/Voxels/Assemblies (experimental), VSM with receiver masks and invalidation throttling.
  - Substrate is production-ready, TSR keeps being refined, Heterogeneous Volumes is still experimental.
- **Unity 6**: APV, the GPU Resident Drawer and the STP upscaler. HDRP is now in maintenance mode, and URP gets 'Surface Cache GI', SSR and GTAO in 6.7 LTS (roadmap). Unity 6.6 made WebGPU production-ready for web builds.
- **AAA games** ship full path tracing with ReSTIR plus a neural denoiser on NVIDIA PC: DOOM: The Dark Ages, Resident Evil Requiem, PRAGMATA, 007 First Light. Capcom's GDC 2026 talk gives 8-20 ms at 1440p on RTX 40-class cards.
- **Upscalers** are now ML upscaling plus multi-frame generation: DLSS 4.5 up to 6x, FSR Redstone / FSR 4.1, XeSS 3, and MetalFX on Apple.
- **Neural shading** (cooperative vectors, NTC, NRC, Metal TensorOps) and DXR 2.0 / Mega Geometry clustered BVHs are mostly demos or SDKs. I found no shipped game using NTC or neural shaders.
- **Gaussian splats** are mainstream on the web: KHR_gaussian_splatting is ratified, three.js r186 has a native WebGPU renderer, and Spark and PlayCanvas support them. Unreal and Unity rely on plugins.

What a small wgpu engine can reach:
- **Browser WebGPU** has compute, subgroups (Chrome), immediates, primitive index and compatibility mode. Bindless and 64-bit atomics are still drafts. There is no ray tracing or mesh-shader proposal. So Nanite-style software raster and any ray tracing are off the table on the web.
- **wgpu 30 on Metal** has experimental ray queries, mesh shaders (full support, WGSL included), subgroups, binding arrays and int64 atomic min/max.
- **wgpu-native 29.0.1.1**, which aipocket pins, offers no BLAS/TLAS API, so hardware ray tracing cannot be built from C++ (same on trunk 2026-09-20). Mesh shaders are not exposed either.

Honest comparison: aipocket has a broad, modern 'forward+ with screen-space effects' stack (clustered lights with shadows, PCSS, SSR, SSGI, probes, DDGI-style visibility volumes, TAA, atmosphere, clouds, water, AgX). Its visible gaps to UE5-class output are:
- No dynamic multi-bounce GI; volumes are static once captured.
- No temporal upscaling.
- No virtualized or dense geometry.
- No ray-traced shadows or reflections.
- No HDR output.

Ranked next steps by visual payoff per effort; all except 7 also run in the browser:
1. **Temporal upscaling inside the existing TAA** (TSR/STP/FSR2-style). Jitter, motion vectors and YCoCg history clipping already exist (rendering.md:901-926), and the dynamic render scale (103-128) currently just stretches. The showcase drops from 5.8 to 1.9 ms at half scale, so this buys either crisper Retina output or about 2x headroom for the items below. About 1-2 weeks.
2. **Dynamic, camera-centred probe GI** (Lumen-Lite/DDGI): keep re-capturing IrradianceVolume probes time-sliced (already 2 a frame, rendering.md:832-836) in cascades that follow the camera, with temporal blending, so GI follows the day cycle, weather and moving lights. Epic shipping exactly this class as Lumen Lite supports the approach. About 2-4 weeks.
3. **Cheap BRDF fixes**: multi-scatter GGX energy compensation, specular occlusion from AO and probe visibility, and GTAO-style AO with bent normals. None was found by name in renderer.cpp. Days of work; rough metals and crevices look right.
4. **HDR/EDR output to the M5's XDR display** (listed under 'Not yet', rendering.md:1104-1105). It needs a wgpu-native newer than 29.x or a patch; wgpu 30 has display_hdr_info. About 1 week once the API is there; very visible on Apple screens.
5. **A Gaussian splat primitive** (KHR_gaussian_splatting import, compute sort, instanced quads; SH0 first, then SH3 and LOD). It fits agent-first worlds built from captures or AI generators. About 2-3 weeks.
6. **GPU-driven culling plus meshlet cluster LOD** (Nanite-lite on hardware raster): compute frustum and Hi-Z culling into indirect draws, clusters from meshoptimizer. It pays off for dense scenes and foliage (hills at 1.1M triangles). About 4-8 weeks. On the web it stays hardware-raster only, since there is no 64-bit atomics, bindless or multi-draw-indirect.
7. **Native-only hardware ray tracing**: RT shadows and reflections, then ReSTIR GI like Bevy Solari or RE Engine. Metal can do it through wgpu 29+, but it needs a wgpu-native C API extension or fork for acceleration structures, plus a denoiser (MetalFX would need native interop). It would never run in browsers. Months of work; defer.

Not realistic now: neural texture compression or neural shading, multi-frame generation, Mega-Geometry-class cluster BVHs.

obj.method:
Done on 2026-10-02 on the Apple M5 / 32 GB machine, using the already-built release runtime build/release/bin/pocket_runtime, which I did not rebuild. A background agent_eval run and another agent were active at the same time, so load averages were 5 to 13 on 10 cores and all timings are noisy. Scratch root is /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-qiulinfan-Desktop-pocketEngine/b7d0fc97-779a-4afb-8145-c566b7e1bb53/scratchpad/render-assessment (called <R> below).

Project setup: I copied samples/hello to <R>/objstress and replaced scripts/main.ts with a sun-only scene. Bundling with `./.pocket/pocket ts <dir>` names the output after project.toml's name, so the first attempt overwrote build/ts/hello.js. I restored it straight away by re-bundling samples/hello, then bundled the scratch project with `--out build/ts/objstress.js`, the name Runtime expects. Nothing in the aipocket working tree changed: git status shows only a pre-existing untracked .codex/.

Generators in <R>/gen:
- scan.c: a lumpy displaced sphere written as v + vn with f a//a; 1M, 5M and 12M triangles.
- machined.py: mm units, Z-up, no vn, welded vertices. A 63x63 drilled plate (64-segment holes) with a square tower and a 48-tooth gear, offset 250,000 mm in x/y; 1.53M triangles. The same script made a 40x40 copy at the origin and one 4,500,000 mm (4.5 km) away.
- assembly.py: 4800 bolt/pin parts with v/vn, flat caps, 5 usemtl materials and an mtllib; about 1.98M triangles. One file uses o per part, the other g per part.
- ngons.py: a quad floor, L prisms, stars, a comb and a C written as single f n-gons, all with negative v/vt/vn indices.
- cube_soff.obj: a welded cube with `s off`.

Driver: measure.py subclasses tools/scripts/dev/runtime.py's Runtime (rpc timeout raised to 900 s) and runs each case in a fresh runtime at 1280x720, headless and paused. The runtime is wrapped in `/usr/bin/time -l` for exact max RSS and peak memory footprint, and `ps -o rss` is also sampled every 100 ms. Sequence per case:
1. step, then spawn a Camera (priority 100, look_at), then render 2 frames.
2. Time `world.spawn {Model, Transform, MeshRenderer:{mesh}}` plus the following `step {ticks:1, render:"each"}`. That interval is the reported load time.
3. Render 30 more frames, then read render.stats, capture, and assets.describe.
4. Turn the model 0.5 degrees per frame for 10 frames so the shadow cascades redraw, then read render.stats and perf again (gpu passes and the CPU render phase).
5. Take extra capture variants: case 3 upright (pitch -90, scale 0.001) and close-ups.

The big cases ran 3 times; I report the median and range. Extra checks:
- split.py times assets.import separately from the spawn.
- freeze.py sends a `state` RPC during a load.
- profile_load.py runs /usr/bin/sample on the runtime during the 5M load.
- fastobj_bench.c is a plain single-threaded mmap reader with corner dedupe, used as a lower bound.
- Blender 4.5.12 LTS ran headless `bpy.ops.wm.obj_import` once per file as a reference (gen/blender_import.py). It also rendered Workbench pictures of ngons, the machined part and the cube from the same cameras (gen/blender_render.py).

I looked at every capture with Read. A summary sheet is at <R>/captures/obj_import_findings_sheet.png. Per-case JSON is in <R>/logs, and /usr/bin/time and sample outputs are next to it.

cases.name: 1. scan_1m (smooth scan surface with vn)
cases.notes: Load: 0.93, 0.96 and 1.05 s (median 0.96). Peak memory footprint 717 MB; RSS after load 438 MB. Renders as 1 draw. GPU when static: scene pass 1.6 ms. With the model turning and shadows redrawn: 2.4 to 3.5 ms (shadow 1.0 to 2.4 ms). The file's vn are used and shading is smooth; the ridge at the left is real geometry, checked in captures/scan_1m_zoom.png. Vertex and triangle counts match Blender exactly. cases.name: 2a. scan_5m (with vn)
cases.notes:
Load: 5.06, 5.24 and 6.08 s. Peak footprint 2.08 to 2.11 GB; RSS after load stays about 1.6 GB because the CPU copy is kept. GPU static scene pass 3.9 to 4.6 ms; turning 7.5 to 10.4 ms (shadow 4.2 to 6.7 ms). The CPU render phase averages 5.4 to 6.9 ms, which is mostly waiting on the GPU.

The runtime does not respond during the load: a `state` RPC sent 0.5 s in was answered 4.6 s later. Profile of the main thread: 870 of 1168 samples at import.cpp:225 (the std::map vertex dedupe at lines 207-227), 131 at import.cpp:148 (splitting lines with istringstream), 12 in fill_tangents. With the existing opt-in `lods:[{screen:4, ratio:0.1}]`, the same view draws 499,950 triangles at 2.5 ms GPU while turning and looks the same (captures/scan_5m_lod.png). The cost is about 1.3 s more load for the simplification. Blender's import takes 3.17 s; the C reader 0.29 s.

cases.name: 2b. scan_12m (with vn)

cases.name: 3. machined_2m (no vn, welded, Z-up, mm, offset 250,000 mm)
3b. machined_far (same part type, 4,500,000 mm = 4.5 km offset, 620k tris) vs machined_near (at origin)

cases.name: 4a. assembly_o (4800 parts, o per part, 5 usemtl, vn)
cases.notes:
Load: 1.92, 1.98 and 2.05 s; peak footprint about 1.25 GB. The file becomes 4800 nodes and 4800 submeshes, which draw as 4800 draw calls and 4800 instances; shadow redraws add 14,400 draws. GPU 5.9 ms static and 7.9 ms turning; CPU render phase 6.2 ms.

There is no culling per part. With the camera inside the assembly looking at one corner (assembly_o_inside), the renderer still draws 4800 parts and 1,984,072 triangles with out_of_view 0.

Materials from the MTL file (Kd, and Ns as roughness) and the flat-cap/smooth-side normals render correctly. The scene has no sky or ambient, so shadows are black. Blender's import takes 1.26 s and makes 4800 objects; the C reader 0.14 s.

cases.name: 4b. assembly_g (same geometry, g per part, no o)
cases.looks_right: yes (pixels), but the part structure is lost
cases.notes:
Load: 1.72, 1.85 and 2.37 s. A g line only creates a node when there is none yet (import.cpp:171-172), so all 4800 parts collapse into 1 node and 5 submeshes, one per material; assets.describe lists 1 part. That cuts drawing to 5 draws (15 shadow draws), GPU 2.4 ms static and 5.8 ms turning, CPU 3.4 ms. The cost is that individual parts can no longer be instantiated, picked or moved.

Many exporters write g for parts (3ds Max, SketchUp and others; unverified per exporter). Blender's import takes 1.09 s and makes 1 object.

assembly_g: 1.09 s / 1.74 s / 1203 MB / 1112 MB (1 object)

aipocket, spawn to first frame, median of 3 (range): scan_1m 0.96 s (0.93-1.05); scan_5m 5.24 s (5.06-6.08); scan_12m 17.1 s (13.5-26.6); machined_2m 1.10 s; assembly_o 1.98 s; assembly_g 1.85 s. That is about 1.6-1.8x Blender's import call at 1M-5M and 1.7-3.3x at 12M.

Lower bound: a plain single-threaded C reader in this scratch dir (gen/fastobj_bench.c: mmap, hand-rolled number parsing, fan triangulation, open-addressing (v,vt,vn) dedupe, 64-byte vertices; no materials, groups or GPU). scan_1m 0.11 s, scan_5m 0.29 s, scan_12m 1.31 s, machined 0.09 s, assembly 0.14 s, with the same unique vertex counts as aipocket. That is 9-19x faster than aipocket's whole load.
Note: `assets.import` on the same files took 1.8 s (1M), 10.2 s (5M) and 20.5 s (12M), longer than the spawn path. I did not investigate why.

issues.issue: Concave polygons are triangulated wrong. Faces with more than three corners are always fanned from the first corner, so a concave n-gon comes out right or wrong depending only on which corner the exporter wrote first.
issues.evidence: import.cpp:194, documented as intended in docs/design/assets.md:174-175 ('faces with more than three corners are fanned'). In case 5, 4 of 8 concave faces render wrong (L from tip, star from outer tip, comb, C sign); Blender renders all 8 correctly. See captures/compare_ngons.png.
issues.fix: Fan only when the polygon is convex; checking that is cheap. Otherwise project the polygon onto the plane of its Newell normal and ear-clip it. That is about 80 lines, or use mapbox earcut.hpp, header-only (URL not checked in this run). Add the case-5 file to assets_tests [obj].

issues.issue: Files without vn are smoothed per position with no crease angle, and `s off` / smoothing groups are ignored. CAD and STL-converted parts with welded vertices therefore render as blobs: boxes look rounded, holes look like studs, sharp edges are smeared.
issues.evidence: The area-weighted smoothing is at import.cpp:198-206 and is used at line 220. The key dispatch at import.cpp:151-195 has no `s` branch. Shown in captures/compare_machined_near.png (Blender flat on the right), machined_closeup.png (the square tower looks like a cylinder) and compare_cube_soff.png. Faceted parts with vn render correctly (assembly caps).
issues.fix: Without vn, compute crease-angle normals: accumulate per face, then give a vertex a separate copy for each fan of faces whose normals are within a threshold, about 30-45 degrees (Blender's default auto-smooth is 30). Treat `s off` / `s 0` as flat and `s N` groups as smoothing groups. Expose the angle as an import option and report it in assets.describe.

issues.issue: Coordinates are parsed and stored as float32, so models far from the origin, such as plant, BIM or GIS coordinates, lose precision at load time. A Transform cannot recover it.
issues.severity: high for CAD/BIM; none below a few hundred metres
issues.evidence: to_float uses strtof (import.cpp:46-50) for v (import.cpp:152), and MeshVertex.position is a float Vec3 (engine/assets/include/pocket/assets/assets.hpp:24). At a 250 m offset there were no visible artifacts. At 4.5 km the 6 mm holes become stair-stepped with noisy normals (captures/compare_offset.png).
issues.fix: Parse v as double. Compute the bounds in double and subtract a double origin (the bounds centre, or a user pivot) before converting to float. Keep that origin as the node's rest translation, or a new Mesh.origin reported by assets.describe, so that world.instantiate and agents can place the part back. Optionally add an import option to keep or drop the offset.

issues.issue: Loading is slow and blocks the main thread. Tokenizing every line with istringstream and deduplicating corners with std::map dominate the time, and the whole runtime (simulation, rendering, RPC) freezes until the parse finishes.
issues.severity: high for 5M+ triangles, medium below that
issues.evidence:
Load times: 0.96 s for 1M, 5.2 s for 5M and 13.5-26.6 s for 12M, against 0.11 / 0.29 / 1.31 s for a plain C reader and 0.54 / 3.17 / 8.09 s for Blender. In the sample profile of the 5M load, 870 of 1168 main-thread samples are at import.cpp:225 (the std::map<std::array<int,3>> at 207-227) and 131 at :148 (split_ws/istringstream, lines 38-44). The text is copied 2-3 times: fs::read_text goes through ostringstream (engine/core/src/fs.cpp:8-14), then parse_obj builds an istringstream (import.cpp:142).

The load is triggered synchronously from world bounds derivation (engine/world/src/world.cpp:1446-1449, through session.cpp:821) into AssetStore::mesh (assets.cpp:2076-2158). A `state` RPC sent during a 5 s load waited 4.6 s.
issues.fix: Rewrite the reader as a single pass over a mmap or string_view: no per-line strings, std::from_chars or fast_float for numbers, and a hash map or flat array for dedupe. When every corner has v==n and no vt, use the position index directly. Group by (node, material) with vectors, not std::map. Then move the import to a worker thread. The world gets placeholder bounds and the renderer draws nothing (or a bounding box) until the mesh is ready, and the RPC answers with a 'loading' state. Parsing chunks in parallel, like Blender's importer, is optional later.

issues.issue: There are no unit or up-axis import options for OBJ. Z-up millimetre models arrive lying on their side and 1000x too big. The Blender-converted formats are turned Y-up, so the engine behaves inconsistently between formats.
issues.evidence: parse_obj applies no axis or unit conversion. The Blender path exports with export_yup=True (import.cpp:536), as the doc says ('Blender's Z-up scenes arrive Y-up', docs/design/assets.md:197). Case 3 renders as a wall (captures/machined.png) until it is given Transform {pitch:-90, scale 0.001, matching position}, after which it is correct (machined_upright.png).
issues.fix: Add per-asset import settings, for example an [assets.import."assets/x.obj"] table in project.toml or assets.import {up:"z", unit:"mm", recenter:true}. Bake them into the mesh, and have assets.describe report the size in metres and suggest an up axis when the bounds look Z-up.

issues.issue: Large assemblies draw one draw call per part, there is no culling per part, and parts written with g only are silently merged.
issues.evidence: Every (o, material) pair becomes its own submesh (import.cpp:116, 188-194, 207-232), and the renderer pushes one draw per submesh (renderer.cpp:11977-12000). Culling uses the whole entity's Bounds, not each part's (renderer.cpp:11877-11880). Measured: 4800 draws, plus 14,400 shadow draws on redraw, about 6 ms CPU. With the camera inside the assembly it still draws 4800 parts and 1.98M triangles with out_of_view 0. With g only, import.cpp:171-172 collapses everything to 1 node / 5 submeshes, so parts cannot be picked or instantiated.
issues.fix: (a) Store bounds per submesh and cull each draw against them. (b) Batch static parts that share a material into one draw, with a part id per vertex or a meshlet-to-part table, so picking and world.instantiate still work. (c) When a file has no `o` lines, treat `g` as parts.

issues.issue: Huge meshes get no automatic LOD and no cluster or meshlet culling, so a 12M-triangle model is one draw that costs the full GPU time whatever is on screen.
issues.evidence: Without MeshRenderer.lods there are no LOD levels (renderer.cpp:11763-11764; docs/design/rendering.md:636-652). scan_12m costs 15-18 ms GPU when the shadow cascades redraw (shadow 8.7-10.6 ms). With the existing opt-in lods ratio 0.1, scan_5m drops to 0.5M triangles and 2.5 ms (from 7.5-10.4 ms) with no visible difference, at about 1.3 s extra simplify time.
issues.fix: Short term: when an imported mesh is over about 1M triangles, add simplified levels automatically, or have assets.describe or world.lint suggest `lods`. Long term: build meshlets at import with the meshoptimizer already vendored (third_party/meshoptimizer 1.3: meshopt_buildMeshlets at meshoptimizer.h:731, meshopt_computeMeshletBounds at :822) and cull clusters by frustum and normal cone, using indirect draws or a compute pass.

issues.issue: Parsed OBJ meshes are not cached, so every runtime start, reload or pack re-parses the text file.
issues.evidence: Every load goes back to parse_obj (assets.cpp:2107-2112). The Blender formats are already cached as .imported/<path>.glb, keyed by size and content hash (import.cpp:555-574, docs/design/assets.md:186-193).
issues.fix: Write the parsed mesh to .imported/<path>.glb (or an engine binary) under the same stamp scheme, and read that when the stamp matches. A packed game then ships the binary and never parses the OBJ. A 12M mesh as binary is about 0.5 GB and loads in well under a second.

issues.issue: Peak memory is about 5.5x the file size, and the full CPU copy of the mesh stays resident after upload.
issues.evidence: Peak footprint was 2.1 GB for 392 MB of text and 5.3 GB for 959 MB; Blender used 2.5 GB and 5.8 GB. RSS after load stays at 1.6 GB (5M) and 2.0-3.0 GB (12M). CPU vertices are 64 B (assets.hpp:23-29) and GPU vertices 40 B (engine/renderer/include/pocket/renderer/primitives.hpp:12-18). During the parse, corners take 36 B per triangle per group, plus the std::map nodes.
issues.fix: This mostly comes for free with the streaming parser and the binary cache. In addition, release the CPU copy of render-only meshes after upload, keeping the positions and indices if mesh colliders or LOD need them, and quantize GPU normals and tangents to save memory.

obj.verdict:
Only partly. Every file loaded, the counts match Blender exactly, negative indices and quads are handled correctly, and smooth scans with vn look right up to 12M triangles. 1-5M triangles render at interactive speed. But typical industrial and CAD exports are not handled well:
- Faceted parts without vn, or with `s off`, are smoothed into blobs.
- Concave n-gons are fanned into wrong shapes.
- Z-up millimetre files arrive lying on their side with no import option.
- Plant or GIS-scale coordinates lose precision at parse because they are read as float32.
- A 5M / 12M-triangle OBJ freezes the whole runtime for about 5 s / 14-27 s. That is roughly 2-3x Blender's import time and 10-20x a plain C reader, mostly because of std::map and istringstream.
- Assemblies draw one draw call per part with no culling per part.
The highest-value fixes are crease-angle normals with `s` handling, ear-clipping for n-gons, a fast parser on a worker thread with a binary cache, a double-precision recenter, up-axis/unit options, and meshlet or per-part culling. The other fixes are listed in issues. All scratch files, about 1.7 GB of generated OBJs (safe to delete), captures and logs are under <R>; the summary picture is captures/obj_import_findings_sheet.png. All runtime processes were quit.
